> **Definition of Bedrock**
>
> In an abstract sense, the main principles on which something is based. [1]
>
> In the real world, the bedrock is the hard area of rock in the ground that holds up the loose soil above. [1]
>
> In many civil engineering projects, the identification of the bedrock through digging, drilling or geophysical methods is an important task, which greatly influences (foundation) design. [2]  
>
> Sources: [[1] Bedrock | Cambridge Dictionary](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english/bedrock), [[2] Bedrock | Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedrock)

Bedrock is an open-source Python library that forms the foundation for for Geotechnical Engineering, subsurface modelling and Geo-BIM.

<!-- Ground investigation data has traditionally been trapped in specialized file formats that limit its accessibility and utility. -->

Ground Investigation (GI) data is often stored in specialized file formats that are not easily accessible for modern (geospatial) analysis and visualization workflows.
Bedrock lets you transform this GI data into structured objects in Python, enabling you to analyze it, and export it to geospatial databases.
This enables integration of GI data with other software and workflows used in the AEC industry.

## Hierarchical Nature of GI data

<!-- TODO: get the definition of Ground Investigation from the British Standard and create a glossary -->
Ground investigation data is information collected about the soil, rock, and groundwater conditions at a site before construction begins.
It includes test results and samples that reveal the ground's properties.
This information helps engineers design safe and suitable foundations while identifying potential risks or hazards.
This is essential for making informed decisions and avoiding problems during construction.

GI data inherently exists in a structured hierarchy. This hierarchy follows how ground investigations are performed.
A project, say a new building or bridge, comprises multiple test locations.
In-situ tests are performed at a specific locations.
One test location can also yield multiple samples from different depths. In turn, these samples may undergo multiple laboratory tests.
These hierarchical relationships can be visualized in a tree diagram like this:

## AGS4 Data

Industry GI data formats like [AGS](/articles/2025-04-14-ags/) implement a hierarchical data structure in text-based files.
AGS does so by organizing GI data into structured tables called "Groups".
Each group represents a specific aspect of a Ground Investigation, for example, project information (PROJ), location details (LOCA), sample information (SAMP), or an in-situ test like a Standard Penetration Test (ISPT).
These groups are organised in a hierarchical manner: samples and in-situ tests belong to locations, which belong to projects, mirroring how ground investigations are conducted.

AGS4 successfully addresses many aspects of GI data organization, but its specialized nature and age creates limitations.

* Its use is limited to geotechnical engineering applications, meaning we can't easily process or view the data using common tools. This also inhibits sharing this data with others in the civil engineering sector.
* One project's data is spread over multiple different files.
* File size inefficiency. Text representation of data requires more storage space than binary formats.

## Geospatial Databases

This hierarchical model aligns closely with [relational databases](https://observablehq.com/blog/databases-101-basics-data-analysts#what-are-relational-databases).
Relational databases organize data in tables with rows and columns.
Tables can be related to each other using keys. A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. 
A foreign key creates a link between tables, allowing data from different tables to be combined and queried efficiently
Relational databases are foundational to modern data management, and probably the most common type of database.

Geospatial databases are extensions of databases that with capabilities for storing, indexing, and analyzing location-based data. These databases add support for standardized coordinate systems to ensure spatial integrity.
These additions enable efficient retrieval and analysis of spatial data.


## Benefits of Geospatial Databases

The purpose of Bedrock is NOT to become THE standard for GI data, because we don't need 15 instead of 14 competing standards:

<figure style="margin-block: 16px; margin-inline: auto; text-align: center;">
  <img src="https://bedrock.engineer/public/images/14Become15Standards.png" alt="14 competing standards become 15 competing standards | xkcd.com/927" width="60%"/>
  <figcaption>Source: <a href="https://xkcd.com/927/" target="_blank">https://xkcd.com/927</a></figcaption>
</figure> 

Rather, Bedrock lets you transform GI data from specialized formats like AGS4 into geospatial databases to overcome these constraints while preserving the hierarchical relationships of the data.
By assigning (3D) geospatial geometry to each of the features in GI data that have a geographic element (like locations, samples, in-situ tests), it becomes a geospatial database.
This lets you bridge the gap between specialized GI data and the wider world of geospatial tools and standards.

Geospatial GI data gives you greater flexibility in utilizing the data.
It makes the data accessible through portable file formats like [GeoPackage](https://www.geopackage.org/) or [GeoParquet](https://geoparquet.org/) or database systems like [PostGIS](https://postgis.net/).
This breaks data silos and unlocks multiple workflows, from Python-based scientific computing for advanced analysis, 3D visualization, and machine learning, to traditional GIS software for mapping.
The same dataset can be used in parametric design tools like Rhino3D or power interactive web maps.

Geospatial databases ensure proper spatial referencing, allowing information to flow across project boundaries.
This supports integration with the broader civil engineering ecosystem and throughout the project lifecycle.
Your subsurface data can connect with BIM environments, to be viewed with above-ground geospatial information like satellite imagery, Digital Elevation Models, and built structures.
This way, Bedrock creates an open-source foundation for more comprehensive project understanding and more informed engineering decisions.
